notes.lumonde: Feminine: une patate douce, des patates douces.
notes.nnina: From avoir: j’ai, tu as, il a.
notes.enjala: Feminine: la faim. J’ai faim, I’m hungry.

guidebook.intro: At the market you’ll name food, say you’re hungry, and buy and sell. French has a few surprises: you “have” hunger, and “no” turns “some” into “de”.

tips.title: J’ai faim: “I have hunger”
body: French uses **avoir** (to have) where English uses “to be”: **J’ai faim** (I’m hungry), **J’ai soif** (I’m thirsty). The same goes for age: **J’ai vingt ans** (I’m twenty).
The forms of avoir: **j’ai, tu as, il a, elle a**. You’ll use them all the time.

tips.title: Du, de la, des at the market
body: Food you don’t count takes **du** (masculine) or **de la** (feminine): **du riz, du poulet, de la viande**. Countable things in the plural take **des**: **des oranges, des haricots**.
After a negative, all of these become **de** (or **d’**): **Je n’ai pas de sœur**, **Je ne veux pas de viande**.
table: Je ne veux pas de thé.
I want tea. / I don’t want tea.
I have oranges. / I don’t have oranges.

tips.title: Saying no: ne … pas
body: French wraps the verb in two words: **ne** before and **pas** after. **Je mange** → **Je ne mange pas**. Before a vowel, **ne** becomes **n’**: **Je n’ai pas faim**.
In everyday speech people often drop the **ne**: **J’ai pas faim**. Write it, but don’t be surprised when you don’t hear it.

culture.title: Le marché
body: Open-air markets are at the heart of daily life across francophone Africa and France. Greet the seller first, ask **C’est combien ?**, and don’t be shy about choosing your own tomatoes.
